title: Mezzrow recordings, Hugues Panassie and Fontainebleau
summary: Welburn reads out the Vogue session titles, and Moore mentions Hugues Panassie's role.

blocks.x: You recorded some pieces with Mezz Mezzrow, it was a sextet, a concert at the Theater Champs Elysee. Let's say, Buck Clayton was with that group, Gene Sedric, Kansas Fields and Red Phillips. It was really, I guess -- if it was March 1st, 1953, it was for the Vogue Record Company. I guess it was around the same time as the "Saints" was recorded that came out on your album.
Well, that same group we did a thing in Strasburg, France, and that's where the "Saints" was recorded on the tape. That's what I got on my album.
I see. They recorded, well, the "Saints" which is "When the Saints go Marching In," but they also recorded "Wabash --
We had Bud Clayton, Red Richards, Gene Sedric, Kansas Fields. And we had a French bass player.
And there was "Wabash Blues," "Muskrat Ramble," "Ain't Misbehaving," "I Can't Believe You're

I see. That became the title of his autobiography.

That's right. Then a month later you went into the studio again and recorded "Wrap your Troubles in Dreams," "Rose Room," "Swinging with Mezz," "St. Louis Blues," "Big Butter and Egg Man," and "I Ain't Got Nobody." Do you remember those dates?

Oh, yes, yes, because Hugues Panassie was handling the bookings along with Mezzrow and Hugues was in our corner, our style of jazz. Incidentally, when Hugues wrote his "Guide to Jazz," or what was it, jazz critic book, I was included in it, he gave me a nice plug in his book. I was a guest at in his house, Fountainbleu."
Fountainbleau, that's where he resided for a number of years.
